I’m an old man now, seventy-one, and I’ve been working this land in Quzhou since I was a boy. My bones know the seasons better than any book. Around here, if you don’t plant winter wheat and summer corn, you’re either foolish or you have some other business I don’t understand. The double crop — wheat first, then maize — is what the land was made for, and it’s what feeds my family and pays for my grandson’s schooling.

This year, I’ll keep all four mu in the wheat–corn rotation. I’m too old to take risks with new crops like vegetables or garlic. The prices jump around, and they need more labor than my back can manage. Wheat and corn have buyers who come right to the village, and the government still gives a small subsidy for grain. I’ll plant the improved wheat seed I bought from the county supply store last autumn — it’s the same variety most of my neighbors use, resistant to lodging and good yield. For the summer corn, I’ll use a hybrid seed; the ears are big and the stalks stand up to the wind.

I don’t do no-tillage. I trust turning the soil. Before sowing wheat, I’ll run the rotary tiller to break up the stubble and make a fine seedbed. For the corn, after the wheat comes off in early June, I’ll till again quickly and plant the same day if I can — every day lost is yield lost.

Fertilizer? I put what I know works. For wheat, about 25 kg of nitrogen per mu, split between base and top-dressing at jointing, plus 12 kg phosphorus and 8 kg potassium. For corn, a bit more nitrogen, around 22 kg, with phosphorus and potassium at about 10 kg each. I irrigate the wheat three times — overwintering water, jointing water, and grain-filling water. The corn gets two good irrigations, one right after planting and one at the big喇叭口 stage. Pesticides? Two sprays for wheat, one for weeds and one for aphids or rust if the weather turns wet. For corn, two sprays, mainly for weeds and the corn borer.

I expect my wheat to bring in about 520 kg per mu if the spring rains behave, and the corn about 630 kg per mu. It’s not fancy, but it’s honest food, and it’s what I know.
